OpenAI says two of its team members built a working hardware device in under a week, with GPT-6 and Astra doing the design.
Astra drew the enclosure, picked the parts, laid out the circuit board and wrote the firmware.
It still needed several rounds of human review before a factory could build it.

threads_text: OpenAI says GPT-6 and Astra designed a working gadget in under a week: the case, the circuit board, the firmware and the interface. The catch: it took several rounds of human review before a factory could actually build it. Would you trust a device designed end to end by AI?

paragraphs.text: OpenAI says two members of its hardware team used GPT-6 and its Astra model to design a working hardware device in under a week. The company described the project on November 3, 2026, in a post about using ChatGPT and Codex for physical engineering, according to The Decoder and Interesting Engineering.

The device gives users a dedicated physical way to talk to Codex, OpenAI's coding agent. It was built as a side project, and the goal was to see whether the models could carry the full hardware development process without direct human edits, Interesting Engineering reported.

According to the reports, GPT-6 set the functional requirements and guided the design. Astra then designed the enclosure, chose the electrical components and laid out the printed circuit board, including where parts sit and how they connect, so that the board fit the case.

Astra also produced the firmware, the user interface and the software that connects the device to Codex, OpenAI said. The Decoder summarized the claim as Astra handling every step from enclosure to interface.
Where people still had to step in

OpenAI acknowledged limits. Astra did not always account for manufacturing constraints, component tolerances and assembly details, so engineers went through several rounds of review and revision before production. A contract manufacturer, which was not named, then produced a small batch of prototypes in less than a month.
The claims come from OpenAI's own account. The Decoder noted that no independent verification of the project has been published.
Wider use inside OpenAI and with partners

OpenAI said its hardware teams already use Codex and ChatGPT to create CAD models, manufacturing drawings and simulations for robotics and computing infrastructure. Token use for that work grew 23 times between February and October 2026, according to the company. Grace Lam, a forward deployed engineer at OpenAI, said Codex speeds up CAD revisions and the conversion of 3D designs into production drawings, Interesting Engineering reported.

On BenchCAD 2.0, a test of whether models can rebuild 3D parts and assemblies and identify connections on circuit boards, GPT-6 Astra at its highest reasoning setting scored 0.594. A newer internal model that OpenAI has not described scored 0.875. The company called the results early evidence rather than proof of mature capability.

OpenAI also named two outside collaborators. Engineers at Chip Ganassi Racing are turning 3D scans of parts into editable CAD models and 2D manufacturing drawings, which can help when original design files are missing. Mazda is working with OpenAI on research into vehicle aerodynamics and crash safety, where Astra explores nose shapes and simulates airflow before Mazda engineers judge the designs against styling and cost.

The project shows how far AI models have moved from writing code toward producing the files that physical products are built from. The repeated review rounds point to the hard part that remains: a design that works on screen still has to survive real tolerances, assembly steps and factory limits, and that knowledge still sits with human engineers.
The next signal to watch is whether OpenAI releases the internal model behind the higher BenchCAD score, and whether partners such as Mazda report results from the aerodynamics work.
